title: Other Desert Cities by Jon Robin Baitz on Broadway #otherdesertcities...
transcript: I am devastated to report that the Ticketmasterification of Broadway is upon us. If last year's Othello prices didn't make it clear, this insanely starry production of Other Desert Cities certainly does. Basically, it's a family drama where Brooke Wyeth comes home for a California Christmas, ready to publish her next book, a memoir which happens to dig up some family skeletons, especially around the loss of her older brother, Henry. Her parents are not too thrilled about this. I won't go further into the plot since it mostly circles this specific conflict, but like many other family dramas, part of the fun is just exploring the character dynamics. The more comedic first act is packed with character exposition, spotlighting Julia Louis-Dreyfus as the icy matriarch and Allison Janney as her dysfunctional sister. Yet as the night wears on and not much time passes in the play either, things begin to stall. The dispute over to publish or not publish the memoir appears to be rooted in ego — a road that can only take you so far. It would be much more interesting to psychologically explore why some family members are so resistant to unpacking their shared trauma, while others feel the need to air it out. The implications of their story being made public weigh heavier by the end of the play, but it takes a while to get there. Aside from my quibbles with the plot, I thought it was a perfectly fine production. It's not always evident that these people are family members, but where the familial chemistry may lack, the script at least presents us a clear archetype of a wealthy and reserved family — one where the kids often refer to their parents by their first names. The individual performances are all pretty good, which is especially necessary in the overly monologue-filled second act. Overall, it's a decent staging of a compelling, albeit dated play, but it lacks both the urgency and the synergy from this cast that it would need to remotely justify these insane, dynamic ticket prices. There's little that's inspiring about this production beyond the names attached to it, and the tickets are so egregiously expensive that you can tell it's catering toward people who would want to see those names, regardless of the quality of the work.
